A.explanation: About $1300 \text{ Hz}$ is close to the frequency shift $\Delta f$, not the full observed frequency $f_o$ which must stay near $122 \text{ kHz}$.

B.explanation: About $1330 \text{ Hz}$ is the calculated increase $f_s v_s / v$, and must be added to $122 \text{ kHz}$ to get the detected frequency.

C.explanation: A frequency below $122 \text{ kHz}$ would mean a longer observed wavelength, which applies to a receding source, not one approaching the microphone.

D.explanation: An approaching source compresses the waves so $f_o = f_s v/(v - v_s)$ gives about $123 \text{ kHz}$, slightly higher than $122 \text{ kHz}$.

hints: Notice the dolphin is the moving source at $16.0 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ towards a stationary observer, with sound speed $1480 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Recall that motion towards the observer shortens the observed wavelength, so the detected frequency must be greater than the emitted $122 \text{ kHz}$.
Use $f_o = f_s \times v/(v - v_s)$ for an approaching source, then check whether your result is just above $122 \text{ kHz}$ or is only the small shift near $1300 \text{ Hz}$.
walkthrough: Identify the Doppler situation: source speed $v_s = 16.0 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ towards stationary observer, wave speed $v = 1480 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, source frequency $f_s = 122 \text{ kHz}$.

State the rule: waves ahead of an approaching source are crowded together, so observed wavelength $\lambda_o = (v - v_s)/f_s$ is smaller and observed frequency $f_o = v/\lambda_o = f_s v/(v - v_s)$ is larger.
Substitute values with units: $f_o = 122 \text{ kHz} \times 1480 \text{ m s}^{-1} / (1480 \text{ m s}^{-1} - 16.0 \text{ m s}^{-1}) = 122 \text{ kHz} \times 1480/1464$.
Calculate the factor: $1480/1464 \approx 1.0109$, so $f_o \approx 122 \text{ kHz} \times 1.0109 \approx 123.3 \text{ kHz}$.
Check sense and options: the result is slightly above $122 \text{ kHz}$, not near $1300 \text{ Hz}$ which is only the shift. This is option D.
